strengths: The paper addresses a timely and practically important problem: generating continuous ground-level panoramic video from satellite imagery and a target trajectory, which is relevant to simulation, digital twins, autonomous driving, and cross-view localization.

The proposed architecture is well motivated at a high level. Combining a tri-plane scene representation, ray-guided pixel attention, and epipolar-constrained temporal attention is a sensible way to inject geometry into cross-view video diffusion.

The VIGOR++ dataset is potentially a valuable contribution because current satellite-to-ground benchmarks mostly support single-image generation rather than continuous trajectory-level video generation.
The paper reports results on both the new video benchmark and established single-image datasets, and includes some useful analysis of temporal attention and downstream localization augmentation.
weaknesses: The technical specification is underdeveloped. Important details such as coordinate calibration, depth sampling ranges, tri-plane initialization for vertical planes from a single overhead image, occlusion handling, pose conventions, and the claimed integration of previously synthesized frames into the tri-plane are not described sufficiently for reproducibility or full soundness assessment.

The video-generation evaluation is not fully convincing. The main baselines are mostly single-image cross-view methods or generic multi-view synthesis methods, while highly relevant satellite-to-ground video or street-view synthesis works are not quantitatively compared. Excluding close prior work due to unavailable code/data weakens the state-of-the-art claim.

The dataset contribution raises significant reproducibility and legal/ethical questions. VIGOR++ is built from Google Maps and Google Street View imagery with manual refinement, but the paper does not clarify redistribution rights, privacy handling, collection time, licensing, or whether the dataset will be publicly released in a usable form.

The metrics and tables are confusing. Metric ordering and directionality are unclear in places, CLIPSIM is treated as lower-is-better despite common usage as a similarity score, and there is no statistical uncertainty or human evaluation for perceptual and temporal quality.

The ablation study is too limited. The paper does not isolate key design choices such as tri-plane versus BEV or height-map priors, CVHA, number/depth of ray samples, use of generated-frame feedback, sequence length, pose noise sensitivity, or whether gains come from epipolar geometry versus sparse local temporal attention.

The method relies on accurate known 4-DoF camera poses and predefined trajectories, but the robustness to realistic pose error, variable trajectory spacing, and out-of-distribution city geometry is not studied.

The writing and positioning need polish: related work omits or under-emphasizes some close comparisons, several equations are underspecified, some claims are stronger than the evidence, and implementation details are deferred to an appendix that is not present in the provided manuscript.

strengths: The paper targets an interesting and practically relevant problem: generating temporally coherent ground-level panoramas from satellite imagery and trajectories.

The proposed combination of satellite-conditioned tri-plane features, ray-guided attention, and epipolar-constrained temporal attention is plausible and conceptually aligned with the geometry of the task.

The paper attempts broad evaluation, including single-image satellite-to-ground benchmarks, a video-generation benchmark, ablations, qualitative examples, efficiency plots, and a downstream localization experiment.
The new VIGOR++ dataset, if released with clear licensing and reproducible construction details, could be useful for the community.
weaknesses: The experimental evidence is not strong enough for a top-tier acceptance. The most directly relevant prior work is not adequately compared: Sat2Vid is cited but not evaluated, and the recent satellite-to-ground video work is excluded due to unavailable code/data despite being the closest setting. The remaining baselines are partly mismatched image-generation or generic multi-view methods.

The claimed geometric consistency is under-supported. The method uses a single satellite image to infer vertical facade/occluded information through a tri-plane, but the paper does not convincingly explain how geometry is learned, calibrated, bounded in depth/height, or validated beyond perceptual metrics.

The ablations are incomplete. The paper compares epipolar attention only against full cross-attention, but does not isolate the tri-plane representation, ray-based sampling, CVHA, use of previous frames projected back into the tri-plane, sparse temporal neighborhood choices, number of sampled ray points, or trajectory length effects.

Reproducibility is weak. The paper states that architectural and implementation details are in an appendix, but no appendix is present in the provided manuscript. Important details such as model size, training schedule specifics, dataset construction pipeline, camera pose normalization, ray depth ranges, attention implementation, and baseline adaptation are missing.

The evaluation metrics are inconsistently presented and sometimes questionable. Several tables mix metric groups and directions in confusing ways, FID values appear unusually small in some settings, CLIPSIM is marked as lower-is-better despite its usual interpretation depending on definition, and the paper does not define exactly how semantic, depth, and temporal metrics are computed for panoramic sequences.

The VIGOR++ dataset raises unresolved concerns. It is built from Google Maps and Street View imagery with manual refinement, but the paper does not address licensing, redistribution rights, privacy, geographic bias, data filtering, or annotation quality control. This is a serious omission for a dataset contribution.

The qualitative evidence is not very convincing. The figures are small, selected examples are limited, and generated panoramas still show visible distortions and inconsistencies. There is no user study or rigorous evaluation of long-range spatial consistency along trajectories.

The downstream localization result is marginal: the reported improvement is small, evaluated on one model and one dataset setting, and lacks variance, significance testing, or comparison to simpler augmentation baselines.

The writing overclaims the contribution. Phrases such as 'faithfully preserves' and 'strong foundation' are stronger than the provided evidence, especially given the under-constrained nature of generating street-level facade content from overhead imagery.

Overall, the paper has an appealing problem and some plausible ideas, but the novelty, comparisons, reproducibility, dataset ethics/licensing, and evidentiary support are not competitive for a top-tier AI conference in its current form.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and timely problem: generating temporally coherent ground-level panoramic video from a single satellite image and a trajectory, which is more ambitious than standard single-view satellite-to-ground synthesis.

The proposed combination of tri-plane satellite-conditioned scene representation, ray-guided pixel attention, and epipolar-constrained temporal attention is well motivated and directly targets the core geometric and temporal challenges of the task.
The new VIGOR++ dataset is a valuable contribution if released with clear licensing, adding large-scale satellite/ground trajectory pairs for a problem where suitable video benchmarks are scarce.
Experiments are reasonably broad: the method is evaluated on VIGOR++ for video generation, on CVUSA/VIGOR for single-image synthesis, and on a downstream cross-view localization augmentation task.

Quantitative results show consistent improvements over several relevant baselines across perceptual, semantic, pixel-level, and temporal metrics; the ablation comparing full temporal attention to epipolar-constrained attention supports the proposed temporal module.
The paper is generally clear, with intuitive figures and a coherent narrative connecting geometry-aware conditioning to temporal consistency.
weaknesses: The evaluation omits or only indirectly addresses some very relevant prior work, especially Sat2Vid and the recent satellite-to-ground video method that is excluded due to unavailable code/data. For a top-tier venue, stronger comparison or at least a careful reproduction/setting discussion is needed.

The ablation study is incomplete. The paper does not cleanly isolate all key components in the full video setting, such as tri-plane representation vs. simpler BEV/plane alternatives, ray-guided attention vs. generic conditioning, temporal attention removal, number of sampled ray points, and sparse-frame choices.

Several technical details are under-specified: how depths along rays are chosen, how tri-plane resolution and feature aggregation are configured, how previously synthesized views are projected back into the tri-plane, and how epipolar constraints are discretized for panoramic images. This weakens reproducibility.

The dataset construction relies on Google Maps/Street View imagery and manual refinement, but the paper does not discuss licensing, release conditions, privacy filtering, or potential geographic/coverage biases. This is a notable unresolved dataset and ethics concern.

The metrics are extensive but not fully convincing for generative realism. No human preference study or task-grounded evaluation of video coherence is provided, and some metric directions/interpretations, such as CLIPSIM being treated as lower-is-better, are unclear.

The downstream localization result is positive but small, with limited details on statistical significance, amount of synthetic data, and whether gains persist across splits or stronger training schedules.

Claims of geometric consistency are stronger than the evidence: the paper reports perceptual/semantic/depth proxy metrics but lacks direct geometric alignment measures, trajectory consistency diagnostics, or failure-case analysis.

strengths: The paper tackles an important and timely problem: generating multiview-consistent 360-degree ground-level panoramas from a single satellite image and a query trajectory. This is a meaningful extension beyond single satellite-to-ground image synthesis and is relevant to simulation, digital twins, and cross-view localization.

The proposed architecture has a coherent design: triplane-based satellite scene encoding, ray-based pixel attention for geometry-aware conditioning, and panoramic epipolar-constrained temporal attention for inter-frame consistency. These components are well motivated by the geometry of the task.

The new VIGOR++ dataset appears valuable, with large-scale satellite/ground-view trajectory pairs across multiple cities, and the paper recognizes the lack of existing benchmarks for continuous satellite-to-ground panorama generation.

The experimental section is reasonably broad: the method is compared against satellite-to-ground and multiview-generation baselines, evaluated on both VIGOR++ sequence generation and standard single-image CVUSA/VIGOR settings, and supported by several ablations.

The reported quantitative gains are consistent across many metrics, including perceptual, semantic, pixel-level, depth, video, and reconstruction-based measures. The ablations support the usefulness of triplanes, ray-based attention, dynamic ray refinement, and sparse epipolar attention.
The downstream cross-view localization experiment, though small, is a nice attempt to demonstrate that generated images can benefit another task rather than only improving image metrics.
weaknesses: The comparison to the most directly related recent methods is incomplete. The paper excludes highly relevant approaches such as Streetscapes and Satellite-to-Groundscape because code/data are unavailable or input settings differ, but this leaves the central sequence-generation claim without comparison to the strongest conceptual competitors.

The dataset construction and reproducibility story are not yet strong enough for a benchmark paper. VIGOR++ relies on Google Maps/Street View data, semi-automatic route extraction, and manual refinement, but the exact collection, filtering, annotation, licensing, and release conditions are underspecified. A promise to release code/data is weaker than an available artifact, especially for a new benchmark.

The geometric formulation has a concerning imprecision: the appendix treats the inverse equirectangular projection P^{-1}(pixel) as a 3D point Q, whereas a panorama pixel only defines a bearing/ray without depth. The epipolar constraint can be formulated over unit bearing vectors, but the proof as written is not technically correct and should be clarified.

Many evaluation metrics are only indirect proxies for the stated goal. Pixel metrics are acknowledged as imperfect, FVD/CLIPSIM may not measure geometric consistency reliably, and the 3D reconstruction metric depends on a learned reconstructor whose failure modes are not analyzed. There is no human preference study or rigorous geometric evaluation using known map/trajectory constraints.

The baseline adaptation details are thin. EscherNet is adapted by treating the satellite image as a source view despite a very different domain and camera model; Sat2Density and ControlS2S are single-image methods extended to sequences. It is unclear whether these baselines are given temporal conditioning, trajectory information, comparable model capacity, and similarly tuned training budgets.

The reported improvements on single-image generation are sometimes modest, especially over ControlS2S on CVUSA/VIGOR, so the novelty and impact depend heavily on the sequence setting where the benchmark is newly introduced by the authors.

The method remains computationally heavy, requiring diffusion sampling and multi-stage training, and the inference/runtime analysis is incomplete beyond selected attention comparisons. Practical scalability to long city-scale trajectories remains uncertain.

Some presentation issues reduce confidence: metric names and directions are occasionally unclear, tables contain formatting inconsistencies, and several claims are stronger than the evidence provided, particularly around 'geometric consistency' and large-scale scene generation.

The broader impacts section acknowledges misuse and safety-critical limitations but remains generic. Given the ability to synthesize plausible geolocated street scenes from satellite imagery, the paper should more concretely discuss privacy, map-data licensing, provenance, and misuse mitigation.

strengths: The paper targets an important and underexplored problem: generating multiview-consistent 360-degree ground panoramas from a single satellite image and a trajectory.
The proposed combination of triplane conditioning, ray-based feature sampling, and panoramic epipolar attention is plausible and reasonably well motivated.
The new VIGOR++ dataset, if released with clear licensing and annotations, could be useful for future work on satellite-to-ground sequence generation.
The paper includes multiple baselines, several quantitative metrics, qualitative results, and ablations for the main modules.
weaknesses: The evaluation is not convincing enough for the strength of the claims. A directly relevant prior work, Sat2Vid, is cited but not compared against, and other recent strong methods are excluded mainly because code/data are unavailable.

Several metrics and table conventions are unclear or inconsistent, e.g. CLIPSIM is treated as lower-is-better, FVD values are unusually small without sufficient explanation, and the 3D reconstruction metrics are not adequately validated as measures of multiview consistency.

The geometric derivation is imprecise: the inverse equirectangular projection is treated as recovering a 3D point rather than a bearing ray with unknown depth. The final epipolar constraint may be standard for rays, but the proof and implementation details are under-specified.

The new dataset construction is a major contribution but is insufficiently documented. The semi-automatic trajectory extraction, manual refinement, pose accuracy, train/test split protocol, and possible leakage or overlap are not described in enough detail.
The reported gains are often modest on single-image generation, and the sequence-generation baselines are not clearly adapted or tuned enough to establish a decisive advantage.

Reproducibility is limited to a promise of future code/data release. Important architectural details, sampling choices, triplane resolution, attention implementation, and evaluation scripts are missing or deferred.
Ethical and legal issues around large-scale Google Maps and Street View data collection, redistribution, privacy, and synthetic misuse are acknowledged only superficially.
The writing has several clarity and formatting issues, and some claims, such as broad applicability to autonomous driving and digital twins, are stronger than the evidence supports.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and challenging problem: generating multiview-consistent 360-degree ground panoramas from a single satellite image and a pose trajectory. This is more ambitious than standard single satellite-to-ground synthesis and is relevant to simulation, digital twins, and autonomous navigation.

The proposed combination of triplane scene conditioning, ray-based pixel attention, and panoramic epipolar-constrained temporal attention is technically well motivated. The method injects useful geometric structure into diffusion-based generation rather than relying only on generic image/video priors.

The new VIGOR++ dataset is a meaningful contribution if released as promised. It substantially expands the setting from paired satellite/panorama images to trajectory-level satellite-to-ground sequence generation, which could enable follow-up work.

The empirical results are broadly convincing: the method improves over adapted baselines on VIGOR++ and shows consistent gains on CVUSA/VIGOR for single-view generation. The ablations on triplane vs. BEV, ray-based attention, dynamic offsets, and sparse temporal attention support the main design choices.

The paper includes several useful evaluation dimensions, including perceptual, semantic, pixel-level, video consistency, and 3D-reconstruction-based metrics, plus qualitative comparisons and a downstream localization experiment.
weaknesses: The comparison set is incomplete for the central claim. Sat2Vid is a directly relevant satellite-to-panoramic-video method cited in the paper but not compared against, and the exclusion of recent methods due to unavailable code/data leaves uncertainty about the true state-of-the-art standing.

Reproducibility is still limited. The paper promises code and dataset release, but key implementation details are underspecified, including exact triplane resolution, sampling parameters, epipolar candidate construction, architecture dimensions, data filtering, and manual refinement protocol for VIGOR++.

The dataset construction raises licensing and distribution concerns because it relies on Google Maps and Street View imagery. The broader impact section mentions misuse but does not adequately discuss dataset redistribution rights, privacy, or terms-of-service constraints.

The evaluation remains partly dependent on imperfect proxies. Pixel-level metrics are weak for an inherently one-to-many generation task, while FVD/CLIPSIM and the Pi3-based 3D metrics may not fully capture geometric correctness. A human preference study or task-specific geometric validation would strengthen the evidence.
The downstream localization result is positive but quite small, so it only weakly supports the claim that the generated data is practically useful for downstream applications.

Some technical presentation issues remain. The panoramic epipolar proof is somewhat imprecise in its treatment of inverse projection and depth, and several equations/metric tables are hard to read due to formatting. The method also relies on known dense pose trajectories and still has slow diffusion inference, limiting practical deployment.
